title: Farm Animals and Their Young
hint: Male, female and young animals; herd, flock, litter; sheep, geese, oxen, cattle
why: farm animals come up everywhere: in stories, on menus, at the zoo with children, on holiday in the countryside. The words for males, females, babies and groups are short but different from animal to animal, and the plurals have some famous traps.
know: the names for the male, the female and the young of common farm animals: bull, cow, calf; ram, ewe, lamb
group words: a herd of cows, a flock of sheep, a litter of piglets
the sounds animals make: moo, baa, oink, neigh, cluck, crow
understand: why we say three sheep and two geese, not sheeps or gooses
why cattle always takes a plural verb: The cattle are in the field.
able: name the animals you see on a farm, and their young
describe a farm visit: what animals there were, how many and what they were doing
talk about farm animals in your country
mistakes: We saw many sheeps in the field.
We saw many sheep in the field.
The cattle is in the field.
The farmer has a big flock of cows.
The farmer has a big herd of cows.
Look at that cow! He's huge.
Look at that bull! He's huge. (a cow is female)
The farmer has twenty pigs. (pork is the meat)
warmup: Which farm animals can you name in English? Make a quick list.
Did you grow up in a city or in the countryside? Have you ever touched a cow, a sheep or a horse?
Which farm animal do you think is the cleverest? Which is the funniest?

the same: one sheep, two sheep
There are forty sheep in the top field.
The geese are very noisy this morning.
The cattle are coming in for the night.
all the farm animals together; no -s
The farm has a lot of livestock.
The cows were mooing at the gate.
The pigs grunted happily in the mud.
The horse neighed when it saw the apples.
The hens cluck after they lay an egg.
The ducks quacked loudly on the pond.

say: SHEEP has a long ee (not ship); in calf the l is silent; in lamb the b is silent; ewe sounds exactly like you; a sow (pig) rhymes with cow.

exercises.title: Who's the baby?
exercises.intro: Match each young animal to its parent. Tap a baby, then tap what it is.

items.why: A calf is a young cow (or bull). The plural is calves.
A lamb is a young sheep. Most lambs are born in spring.
A piglet is a young pig. A sow often has ten or more piglets at a time.
A foal is a young horse. Its mother is a mare.
A kid is a young goat. (Kid is also an informal word for a child.)
A chick is a baby chicken that has just come out of the egg.
A duckling is a young duck. The -ling ending means small or young.
A gosling is a young goose. It has the same -ling ending as duckling.
Sheep is the same in the singular and plural: one sheep, three sheep.
Sheep (and birds like hens and geese) live in a flock. Cows and horses live in a herd.

items.post: in the field near the river.
items.why: Cattle is always plural, so use are: The cattle are in the field.
A litter is a group of babies born together to one mother: a litter of piglets or puppies.

items.pre: A male horse is called a
items.why: A stallion is a male horse. A mare is a female horse, and a foal is a young one.
Goose has an irregular plural: one goose, two geese.
A rooster is a male chicken, and roosters crow. Hens cluck.

items.answer: Our hens lay about twenty eggs a day.

items.answer: A young goat is called a kid.

exercises.title: Reading
exercises.text:
A weekend on my cousin's farm

Last weekend I visited my cousin Marta on her family farm near Guelph, Ontario. I'm a city person, so everything was new to me.

The farm has a herd of about sixty dairy cows. They are milked twice a day, at six in the morning and five in the afternoon. Marta also keeps a small flock of sheep. The ewes had their lambs in March, so the lambs were already running and jumping in the field. My favourite animal was a new calf. She was only two days old, and she followed me everywhere.

Behind the barn there are about forty hens and one very loud rooster. He crowed at half past four on Sunday morning, so I didn't get much sleep! Marta's children collect the eggs every afternoon. There are also two pigs, a sow and a boar. The sow is going to have piglets next month.

Next time I want to stay for a whole week. Farm life is hard work, but I loved it.
exercises.intro: Read the blog post. Then type the missing word from the text, and press Check.

items.why: Paragraph 2: 'The farm has a herd of about sixty dairy cows.'
Paragraph 2: 'The ewes had their lambs in March.'
Paragraph 2: 'She was only two days old.'

items.why: Paragraph 3: the rooster 'crowed at half past four on Sunday morning'.

items.ask: What is the sow going to have next month?
items.why: Paragraph 3: 'The sow is going to have piglets next month.'

exercises.title: Speaking
items: Have you ever visited a farm? What animals did you see? If not, which farm animal would you most like to see up close?
Which farm animals are common in your country? Is any animal special in your culture or in your cooking?
What sounds do animals make in your language? Compare them with English: a cow says moo, a rooster says cock-a-doodle-doo.
Would you like to keep a few hens or a goat at home? Why or why not?

parts.rule:
Watch out

  • the same: one sheep, two sheep; one deer, two deer
  • changes: goose → geese, mouse → mice, ox → oxen, calf → calves
  • add -s: most animals: hens, goats, horses
parts.intro: How does each word make its plural? Sort them.

chips.why: One sheep, two sheep: the plural is the same.
One deer, ten deer: the plural is the same.
One bison, a herd of bison: the plural is usually the same.
One goose, two geese: the vowel changes.
One mouse, two mice: an irregular plural.
One ox, two oxen: an old plural ending, like children.
One calf, two calves: f changes to v, then add -es.
One hen, two hens: a regular plural.
One goat, two goats: a regular plural.
One horse, two horses: a regular plural.

items.q: We saw three sheeps in the field.
items.why: Sheep is the same in the plural: three sheep.

items.q: The cattle is eating grass by the river.
items.why: Cattle is always plural: The cattle are eating grass.

items.q: A young horse is called a foal.
items.why: Correct: a foal is a young horse.

items.q: The farmer has a flock of cows.
items.why: Cows live in a herd. A flock is for sheep and birds.

items.q: Two calfs were born last night.
items.why: Calf has an irregular plural: one calf, two calves.

teacher.purpose: give general learners the core words for farm animals: the animal, the male, the female, the young and the group (bull, cow, calf, a herd), the sounds they make, and the plural traps (sheep, geese, oxen, calves, cattle, livestock). It is the base for the rest of the Farm English lessons.
teacher.before: find three or four photos of farm animals with their young (a ewe and lambs, a sow and piglets, a hen and chicks). Or ask the student to bring a photo of a farm or farm animal from their own country.
plan: The three warm-up questions. Write down every animal the student already knows in English, and note any they say in their own language.

Go through the first table by animal (across), then test by column: “What's a female pig?” “What's a group of cows?” Use your photos. Then the tricky plurals, then the sounds (students usually enjoy making them).
Matching, then the plurals and group words. In Exercise 2, ask why after each answer: sheep is the same, cattle is plural.
Do one together and set the other for home.
The farm blog. First ask: “How many kinds of animal does Marta have?” (five: cows, sheep, hens with a rooster, pigs, and the calf and lambs as babies). Then the questions.
Questions 1 and 2 are the core. Ask follow-ups that need the plurals: “How many sheep?” “Were there any geese?”
Exercise 7 Part A together; Part B at home.
pron: sheep /ʃiːp/ vs ship /ʃɪp/: the long vowel matters. Many learners say ship.
calf /kɑːf/ (North American /kæf/): the l is silent, as in half. calves /kɑːvz/.
lamb /læm/: the b is silent, as in climb and thumb.
ewe /juː/: exactly like you. Students often try to say every letter.
sow (a female pig) /saʊ/ rhymes with cow; sow (to plant seeds, Lesson 4) /səʊ/ rhymes with go.
mistakes: cattle is plural only: the cattle are, forty head of cattle (farmers count cattle as head). Never a cattle or cattles. For one animal, say a cow, a bull or a steer.
livestock: all the farm animals together. No -s, no a. You may hear both livestock is and livestock are; both are fine.
cow is female. In everyday speech people call any cattle “cows”, but a male is a bull. A young male raised for meat is a steer (B2).
chicken is the general word (and the meat). Hen = female, rooster = male. In the UK cockerel is also common; in North America say rooster, because cock is also slang.
pig / pork, cow / beef, sheep / lamb, mutton: live animal vs meat. Lesson 6 covers this; just flag it if the student says porks.
Spanish ganado, French bétail, German Vieh can mean cattle or livestock. Check which one the student means: cattle are only cows and bulls.
kid = a young goat, and also an informal word for a child. Students find this funny; it helps them remember it.
uk_us: Say rooster everywhere; it is understood in the UK too.
Both are fine for general learners.
adapt: Focus on cows, sheep, pigs, horses and chickens: male, female, young. Groups: herd, flock. Plurals: sheep, geese, calves, cattle.
All animals and groups; add steer, heifer (a young cow that has not had a calf), gaggle, a pair of oxen, forty head of cattle.
Describe a farm visit or photo: what animals, how many, what they are doing.
Compare farm animals in two countries, or explain why some animals are special in their culture (e.g. cows in India, horses in Mongolia).
prompts: Have you visited a farm? Follow up: “How many cows were there?” “Were there any babies?” “What were the animals doing?” Listen for sheeps and the cattle is.
Farm animals in your country. Follow up: “Which animal is the most important for farmers there?” “Do people eat it, use its milk or use it for work?”
Animal sounds in your language. A light, fun task. Follow up: “What does a rooster say in your language?” Compare with cock-a-doodle-doo.
Hens or a goat at home? Good for reasons: because, so, but. Follow up: “What would you need?” “What would your neighbours say?”

bank.q: My grandmother kept a small ___ of hens in her garden.
bank.why: Hens, like sheep, live in a flock. A herd is for cows and horses.

bank.q: Five young ___ were following their mother across the road.
bank.why: A young duck is a duckling; five of them are ducklings.

bank.q: The ___ are waiting by the gate for their evening hay.
bank.why: Cattle is already plural: the cattle are waiting. Never cattles.

bank.q: A female horse is called a ___.
bank.why: A mare is a female horse. A stallion is male and a foal is young.

bank.q: We counted fifty ___ in the field behind the farmhouse.
bank.why: Sheep is the same in the plural: fifty sheep.
A ram is a male sheep. A ewe is female, and a lamb is young.

bank.q: Look at those ___! They're trying to eat my sandwich.
bank.why: One goose, two geese: an irregular plural.

bank.q: Our neighbour's ___ starts crowing before the sun comes up.
bank.why: Roosters (male chickens) crow. Hens cluck.

bank.q: A young goat is called a ___.
bank.why: A young goat is a kid.
Mouse has an irregular plural: mice.

bank.q: Our cow had twin ___ last night: a male and a female.
bank.why: A young cow is a calf; two of them are calves (f changes to v).

bank.q: A female pig is called a ___.
bank.why: A female pig is a sow (it rhymes with cow). A male pig is a boar.

bank.q: In spring the ewes give birth to their ___.
bank.why: Ewes (female sheep) have lambs, usually in spring.

bank.q: I saw a beautiful white stallion with her new foal.
bank.why: A stallion is male. The mother of a foal is a mare.

bank.q: There are two oxes pulling the cart.
bank.why: Ox has an old plural: one ox, two oxen.

bank.q: The cattle are resting under the trees.
bank.why: Correct: cattle is plural, so the cattle are.

bank.q: My uncle raises bison on his farm in Alberta.
bank.why: Correct: bison is the same in the singular and plural.

bank.a: How many piglets did the sow have?
bank.why: Question order: How many + noun + did + subject + verb?

bank.a: The children feed the chickens every morning.
alt: Every morning the children feed the chickens.
bank.why: Subject + verb + object + time: The children feed the chickens every morning.

bank.a: A male duck is called a drake.
bank.why: To give a name, use is called: A male duck is called a drake.
